passages.t: ‘The LORD said to my Lord: Sit at My right hand’
passages.happening:
Psalm 110 is short, only seven verses, but it may be the most important psalm for the New Testament. The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). Then a voice reports what God has said.

“The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’” (verse 1).

So there are two figures. ‘The LORD’ is God, speaking. ‘My Lord’ is a king, the one God invites to sit beside him. God promises to put the king's enemies under his feet.

Then God gives him power to rule. “The LORD extends Your mighty scepter from Zion: ‘Rule in the midst of Your enemies’” (verse 2). Zion is Jerusalem. The king's people will come willingly on the day of battle, dressed in holy splendour (verse 3). The last part of verse 3, about ‘the womb of the dawn’ and ‘the dew of Your youth’, is some of the hardest Hebrew in the Psalms. It seems to picture the king, or his young warriors, fresh and strong like the dew that falls at sunrise.
passages.hearers:
Notice the two words for God. In English Bibles ‘LORD’ in small capitals stands for God's own name, as the book page explains. ‘Lord’ in ordinary letters is a different Hebrew word, meaning ‘master’. It is the word a servant used of his master, or a subject of his king.

To sit at a king's right hand meant to hold the place of highest honour and share his power. When Solomon was king, he had a throne brought for his mother, “who sat down at his right hand” (1 Kings 2:19). Here God himself gives that seat to the king.

A footstool under the feet was a picture of complete victory. In the ancient world a conquered enemy was sometimes pictured lying under the victor's feet.

Many scholars think the psalm was first spoken when a new king of David's line was crowned in Jerusalem. A prophet or priest would speak God's word over him: sit, rule, conquer. The book page's part on the royal psalms describes this reading. Others hold, with the heading, that David himself wrote it about a king greater than himself. That question matters for how verse 1 is read, as the hard part below explains.

Most psalms are people speaking to God. Psalm 110 is mostly God speaking about his king. It sounds like a prophet's message.
passages.later:
The book page says that the first verse of this psalm is the Old Testament verse quoted or echoed most often in the New Testament.

Jesus asked the Pharisees a question about it. “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?” They said, ‘David's.’ He answered, “How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’?” (Matthew 22:42-43). If the Messiah is David's descendant, why would David call him his master? “No one was able to answer a word” (Matthew 22:46). The note on Mark 12 on this site explains the argument.

At Pentecost Peter quoted verse 1 and said, “For David did not ascend into heaven” (Acts 2:34). He read it of Jesus, raised and seated at God's right hand. Hebrews asks, “Yet to which of the angels did God ever say: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’?” (Hebrews 1:13). Paul says that Christ “must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).
passages.hard:
Who is ‘my Lord’ in verse 1? Jewish and Christian readers have answered differently, and each reading deserves respect.

Jewish readers have given several answers. The Talmud reads the psalm as spoken about Abraham, whom God made a priest (it uses verses 1 and 4 this way). Some medieval Jewish teachers, among them Abraham ibn Ezra and David Kimhi, read it as a poem written about David by one of his poets, so that ‘my lord’ is King David himself. Some rabbinic writings also read verse 1 of the King Messiah who is still to come. Many modern scholars read it as words spoken over a king of Judah at his crowning.

Christians read it as the New Testament does: David, speaking by the Spirit, called a coming king his Lord, and that king is Jesus. They believe that Jesus, a descendant of David, was raised from the dead and seated at God's right hand. Paul says Jesus was “a descendant of David according to the flesh” and “declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3-4). Some Christian scholars hold that David wrote the psalm, as the heading says; others think it was first a crowning song that said more than any king of Judah ever was, and so came to point forward.

Neither reading is dishonest. Both communities read these words with care. They part over who Jesus is, and that difference is real and is best named plainly and with respect, as the book page says.
passages.asks:
Jesus used this psalm to stretch people's picture of the Messiah. He is David's son, and he is more. Ask whether your own picture of Jesus has grown small: a good teacher, a helper, a friend, but not Lord.

Verse 1 also asks for patience. The king sits ‘until’ his enemies are put down. Not everything is put right yet. Christians live in that ‘until’, trusting the one who is seated.

passages.t: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’
passages.happening:
Verse 4 is the centre of the psalm. God makes a promise with an oath. “The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’” (verse 4).

So the king God seats at his right hand is also a priest. And he is not a priest for a few years, but forever. And he is not a priest by being born into the right family. He is a priest ‘in the order of Melchizedek’, that is, after the pattern of Melchizedek.
passages.hearers:
This would have surprised an Israelite. In Israel, kings and priests were kept apart. Kings came from the tribe of Judah. Priests came from the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron. When King Uzziah tried to burn incense in the temple, he was struck with a skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).

So how could a king of David's line be a priest? The psalm reaches back before Levi was born. Melchizedek was king of Salem and “priest of God Most High” in the days of Abraham (Genesis 14:18). He blessed Abraham, and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. Salem is usually taken to be Jerusalem. The note on Genesis 14 on this site tells his story.

Melchizedek is named only twice in the Old Testament: in Genesis 14 and here. The psalm takes that brief king-priest and makes him the pattern for the king in Jerusalem.

An oath from God was the strongest promise the Bible knows. ‘Will not change His mind’ closes the door on any going back.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews builds a long argument on this one verse, from chapter 5 to chapter 7. It quotes it more than once: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 5:6). It says that Jesus became a priest “not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16).

Hebrews draws out what ‘forever’ means. Ordinary priests died and others took their place. “But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood” (Hebrews 7:24). “Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

The note on Genesis 14 sets out what Hebrews says about Melchizedek and what it does not say.
passages.asks:
A priest stands between God and people. He brings their prayers and offerings to God, and brings God's blessing to them. Psalm 110 promises a king who is also that kind of go-between, forever.

Christians believe that this is what Jesus is now. Hebrews says he ‘always lives to intercede’. If you find it hard to pray, or feel far from God, verse 4 says there is someone who prays for you, and whose priesthood does not end.

passages.t: ‘He will crush kings in the day of His wrath’: battle poetry
passages.happening:
The psalm ends with a picture of victory. “The Lord is at Your right hand; He will crush kings in the day of His wrath” (verse 5). He judges the nations and defeats their rulers far and wide (verse 6).

Notice that the right hand has changed. In verse 1 the king sat at God's right hand. Now God is at the king's right hand, standing beside him in battle.

The last verse is quieter. “He will drink from the brook by the road; therefore He will lift up His head” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
These verses are battle poetry from the ancient world. Kings in that age went to war, and their songs spoke of defeated enemies in strong, bloody pictures. A first hearer would hear in them God's promise that his king would not be overcome.

Verse 6 is hard Hebrew, and translations differ in places. Its meaning in general is clear: God judges, and the proud rulers who stand against him fall.

Verse 7 probably pictures a warrior who stops in the chase to drink from a stream by the way, and then lifts his head, refreshed. Some scholars connect it instead with a crowning rite at a spring. ‘To lift up the head’ was a Hebrew way to say ‘to be restored’ or ‘to be honoured’.

No modern nation or war is in view in these verses. They speak of God's anointed king in ancient Israel and, as Christians read them, of God's final judgment of evil. They give no one today a reason to fight in God's name.
passages.later:
The book of Revelation pictures Christ's final victory with a sword from his mouth: “And from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations” (Revelation 19:15). The weapon is his word.

Jesus told the high priest at his trial, “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62). He was joining Psalm 110 to Daniel 7.
passages.asks:
The psalm promises that evil will not have the last word. God will judge it, in his time. That is a comfort to anyone who has been crushed by the powerful.

It also asks for humility. The victory belongs to God and to his king, not to us. Christians do not fight for it with swords. They wait for it, pray for it, and live under the one who is seated at God's right hand.
